name: Rave

influenced_by: the UK's 1988 "Second Summer of Love" warehouse party scene

media.title: Energy Flash (Simon Reynolds, 1998)
media.note: a widely cited history of the scene, published as a book

reacts_against: licensed club culture's closing hours and legal restrictions, building an illegal, word-of-mouth warehouse-party scene explicitly outside the mainstream nightlife industry.
revivals: a sustained influence on commercial EDM festival culture from the 2000s on
article: UK rave culture detonated almost overnight in 1988, a year British music press nicknamed the "Second Summer of Love" for how closely its mass, euphoric, chemically assisted dancing echoed 1967's hippie summer two decades earlier. Acid house records, imported from Chicago, provided the soundtrack, and a loose network of organizers threw illegal parties in empty warehouses and fields specifically to dodge licensing laws that would have shut a legal club down at 2 a.m. — rave's all-night, often outdoor character was as much a legal workaround as an aesthetic choice. The visual language that grew up around it (fluorescent plastic, glow sticks, the smiley face borrowed from acid house) was built for darkness and strobe light rather than daylight photography, which is part of why rave's palette reads as so aggressively saturated: it had to compete with a blacklight. The UK government's 1994 Criminal Justice Act specifically targeted unlicensed raves and their "repetitive beats," effectively ending the illegal warehouse scene's golden period, but rave's visual and musical DNA fed directly into the much larger, fully legal EDM festival industry that emerged in the 2000s.
